title: Lendy and Prelendy

lessons.title: Land and Preland: The Difference and Why Each Is Needed

teach.title: The Role of a Landing Page in a Link Building Strategy
teach.body: In M03, we learned about the concepts of landing pages and pre-landing pages as elements of the funnel [→ Lesson 3.1]. The CTR of the creative determines how many people clicked on it. The CR of the landing page determines how many of those who clicked took the desired action. Poor creative and a good landing page = few clicks but a high conversion rate among those who visited. Good creative and a poor landing page = many clicks but few conversions. You need both.

teach.title: Landing Page
teach.body:
**Landing Page (Lend)** — the final landing page where conversion takes place. This is where a visitor submits a request, places an order, or performs another target action.

A landing page is not a catalog website or a corporate page. It’s a single page with one goal: to lead the user to a conversion. No unnecessary links, menus, or distractions.

**What a landing page should include:**
- A strong headline highlighting the main benefit
- Confirmation of expectations through creative messaging (Message Match)
- A description of the product and its advantages (benefits, not specifications)
- Social proof (reviews, ratings, number of buyers)
- An order form or button
- Guarantees and security (cash on delivery, returns)

teach.title: Preland
teach.body:
**Pre-landing Page (Intermediate Page)** — an intermediate page between an ad and a landing page. A user lands here after clicking, goes through a “warm-up” process, and only then proceeds to the landing page for conversion.

The goal of the pre-landing page is not to sell (that’s the landing page’s job) but to prepare the user: build trust, deepen their understanding of the problem, and present a solution in such a way that they want to buy even before they see the order form.

**Types of pre-landing pages:**

**Article (Advertorial)** — the most common for e-commerce and affiliate marketing. It looks like editorial content: “10 Causes of Back Pain and What to Do About Them.” A link to the landing page is included in the body or at the end of the article. The more it resembles a real article, the higher the conversion rate (CR). People trust editorial content more than overt advertising.

**Quiz (Survey)** — a series of questions that “qualify” the buyer. “Describe your problem → age → activity level → get a personalized recommendation.” After the quiz, there’s a link to a landing page with a “personalized” solution. High engagement = higher CR.

**Testimonial** — a page in the form of a personal story. “How I got rid of my back pain in 2 weeks.” High trust if the testimonial looks authentic.

**Comparison** — a comparison of several products where the advertised product comes out on top. “Comparing 5 remedies for joint pain.”

teach.title: When You Need a Pre-Land
teach.body:
**Required:**
- The product requires an explanation or "warm-up" before purchase (internal workings, complex mechanisms)
- Direct advertising for the product does not pass Facebook moderation
- The conversion rate (CR) on the direct landing page is low, and you want to improve it
- The audience is “cold” and not ready to buy on the first click

**Not needed:**
- A simple and straightforward product (phone case, kitchen gadget)
- Retargeting—people are already familiar with the product
- The conversion rate (CR) on the direct landing page is already good

l1.q: What is the main function of a pre-loan?
options: Replace the landing page to save on development costs
Warm up and prepare the audience before the final checkout page
Bypass a Facebook pixel
Increase the number of views

l1.q: Mediabuyer is promoting a simple product—a silicone phone stand. Is a pre-launch campaign necessary?
options: That's right—a pre-loan always increases the CR
Most likely not—the product is straightforward, and direct advertising on the landing page is sufficient
That's right—Facebook requires a pre-landing page for all products
It depends on the budget

l2.situation:
Offer A: Pain relief cream. Direct ads are being rejected due to medical claims. Conversion rate (CR) on the direct landing page is 1.2%.
Offer B: Phone case. CR is 5%. Ads are currently undergoing moderation.
Offer C: Weight-loss capsules. The audience is unfamiliar with the brand. Facebook strictly moderates this topic.
Offer D: Retargeting people who have already visited the cream’s landing page.

options: Offer B
Offer G
Offers A and B—both require a warm-up period and have moderation issues
They're all the same

questions.q: Why doesn't Offer G need a preland?
options: Retargeting does not support pre-landing pages
People are already familiar with the product—there’s less need for additional promotion; it’s more important to remind them and give them a reason to come back
The CTR for retargeting is always low
Facebook automatically selects the page type

lessons.title: The Structure of a Conversion-Oriented Landing Page

teach.title: The Principle of a Single Goal
teach.body:
A good landing page is one with a single goal. Every element on the page should lead to one action: submitting a request or placing an order.

A common mistake is adding links to other pages, social media, or menus on the landing page. Every unnecessary link is an opportunity for a visitor to “leave” without converting.

teach.title: Landing Page Structure (Top to Bottom)
teach.body:
**Block 1: Headline (Above the fold)**
The first thing a person sees without scrolling—it must answer the questions “What is this? and Why do I need it?” within 3–5 seconds.

Strong headline: specific result + timeframe + no risk.
“Get rid of back pain in 7–10 days—no pills or injections”

Weak headline: “SpineRelief Cream—Official Website”

**Block 2: Subheading**
Expands on and reinforces the headline. “SpineRelief penetrates deep into the muscle layers and eliminates the cause of pain—it doesn’t just mask the symptoms.”

**Block 3: Main Visual**
An image of the result or product in context. A woman moving freely after applying the cream—better than just a photo of the tube.

**Block 4: Benefits**
Not features—benefits. Not “contains collagen” but “restores joints and reduces inflammation in 20 minutes.”

3–5 points. Each one should highlight a specific benefit for the user.

**Section 5: Social Proof**
Testimonials from real people with their names, photos, and specific results.

Weak testimonial: “Very good cream! I recommend it.”—Irina
Strong testimonial: “My left lower back has been hurting for 3 years. After 10 days of use, I can bend over and play with my grandchildren without pain.” — Maria, 58 years old

**Block 6: Order Form**
Minimum required fields. For COD orders: name + phone number. Period. Every extra field lowers the conversion rate (CR).

Studies show: every additional field in the form reduces the conversion rate by 11–50%, depending on the type of field.

**Block 7: Guarantees and Security**
Alleviates fears and doubts. “Pay on delivery—you pay only when you have the product in your hands.” “Free shipping.” “14-day returns, no questions asked.”

**Block 8: CTA Button**
Large, high-contrast, with specific text.
“Order with a 30% discount” > “Confirm” > “Submit”

teach.title: Message Match — Alignment Between Creative and Landing Page
teach.body:
If the creative mentions a 40% discount, that discount must be featured on the landing page. If the creative shows knee pain, the landing page headline should be about knees—not “joints in general.”

A disconnect between the ad’s promise and the reality of the landing page = a drop in conversion rate. The user feels deceived and closes the page.

l1.q: The order form asks for: first name, last name, phone number, email, address, city, ZIP code, and comments. Is there a problem?
options: The form is too small
Too many fields—each extra one lowers the CR. For COD, just the name and phone number are enough
Email is required for confirmation
No problem

l1.q: Creo promises a "40% discount today only," but there's no discount on the landing page. What will happen?
options: People won't notice the difference
The gap between promises and reality will erode trust and CR
Facebook will automatically remove such ads
CR will increase because people are already interested after the creative campaign

l2.situation:
Scenario — Media Buyer Landing Page:
- Headline: "SpineRelief — Back Cream"
- Large block describing the ingredients (500 words)
- Form: first name, last name, email, phone number, address, city, ZIP code
- One review without a photo: “Very good cream” — Irina
- Button: "Confirm"
- Shipping information — small text at the bottom

CTR 3.1%, CR 0.7%

options: A weak headline with no benefit
Too many fields in the form
Weak social proof
The "Confirm" button isn't very motivating
Shipping information is located at the bottom
Replace the team with a better one
Simplify the form to just the name and phone number, and rewrite the headline to focus on the result
Add more reviews
Change the button color

teach.title: Introductory Article
teach.body:
**Structure:**

**Headline:** addresses the issue without explicit advertising.
"Why Even Young People Experience Back Pain—and What Really Helps"
"An Orthopedist Explains Why Pain Pills for Joint Pain Are a Trap"

**Introduction (2–3 paragraphs):** The reader recognizes themselves in the situation described. Describe specific details of the pain and the limitations it causes—“I can’t pick up my child,” “I can’t sleep properly,” “Pills only help for 2–3 hours.”

**Main Body (3–5 paragraphs):** Useful information that builds trust. Explain the causes of the pain, common mistakes people make (treating symptoms rather than the cause), scientific data, or an expert’s opinion. This isn’t an ad—it’s helpful content.

**A natural transition to the product:** “A new approach has recently emerged…” or “One of the methods showing good results is the topical application of medications that…”

**Product presentation (2–3 paragraphs):** The product as the logical solution to the problem described in the article. Not a list of benefits—an explanation of WHY this particular approach solves the problem better.

**Social proof:** 2–3 testimonials from real people with specific results.

**CTA:** “Learn more and get a discount →” or “Proceed to checkout →.” A gentle transition—not “Buy now,” but an invitation to learn more.

**Key principle:** The article should read like editorial content, not an advertisement. If the first paragraph sounds like an ad, the conversion rate (CR) will be poor. If it looks like a helpful article, the CR will be significantly higher.

teach.title: Quiz-Prelend
teach.body:
**Structure:**

**Landing Page:** "Find out which remedy is right for your type of pain" + "Start the Test" button (high click-through rate—people are curious to find out their "personalized" solution).

**3–5 questions:** about the location of the pain, duration, activity level, age, and previous treatment attempts. The questions should be relevant to the product.

**Results Analysis:** “Analyzing your answers…” animation (2–3 seconds—enhances the sense of a personalized approach).

**Results:** “Based on your answers, we recommend...” + a product description explaining why this specific product is right for this person.

**CTA:** Redirect to the landing page.

**Why quizzes increase conversion rate (CR):** the engagement and accountability effect. The user spent 2–3 minutes answering the questions—they are psychologically more engaged. A personalized result builds trust in the recommendation.

teach.title: Technical Requirements for the Pre-Land
teach.body:
- Fast loading (up to 3 seconds) — critical for mobile
- Mobile optimization — most traffic comes from phones
- No links to external resources other than the target landing page
- No navigation menu—only a CTA to the landing page
- The domain is clean and verified via the Facebook Debugger

l1.q: Why should a pre-release article look like an editorial piece?
options: Facebook blocks pages that look like ads
People trust editorial content more—higher trust = higher CR
Articles are indexed better by Google
The ad style increases CPC

l1.q: Quiz-pre-roll ads have a higher conversion rate than direct advertising. The main reason:
options: The quiz takes longer, and Facebook displays the ad for longer
A person who answers a question is more psychologically engaged, and a personalized result increases trust in the recommendation
Quizzes generate greater organic reach
Facebook algorithmically prioritizes quiz pages

l2.situation:
Scenario:

Landing Page A: "Buy FlexiJoint cream at a 30% discount!" Product photo. List of ingredients. "Order" button. CR 0.9%.

Landing Page B: “A rheumatologist explains why joints hurt even in people without arthritis.” A 400-word article explaining the causes of pain. Natural transition to the product. 2 reviews. CTA: “Learn about the solution →.” CR 3.6%.

questions.q: Why does Preland B have a CR that is 4 times higher?
options: It's longer, so people read more
It builds trust through useful content and looks like editorial material—people arrive at the landing page already "warmed up"
It has more keywords
A rheumatologist's authority automatically translates into

questions.q: Why did Preland A fail despite the discount?
options: The discount is too small
It looks like a direct advertisement—the person doesn't trust it yet and closes the page
The list of ingredients is off-putting
The "Order" button is too pushy

lessons.title: Where to Find Lendys and Prelendys

teach.title: From the affiliate network
teach.body:
Most networks provide ready-made landing pages—and sometimes pre-landing pages—for each offer. This is ideal for an initial test.

**Pros:** It’s fast, requires no effort on your part, and the landing page has already been tested by the advertiser.

**Cons:** Hundreds of other arbitrageurs are using the same page. Facebook may “recognize” this page and lower its trust score. You have no control over conversion rate (CR) optimization.

**Strategy:** For the first test, use a landing page from the affiliate network. If the conversion rate is low or you want to improve it, test your own variations.

teach.title: Website Builders
teach.body:
**Tilda** — the most popular landing page builder among arbitrageurs. Drag-and-drop, hundreds of blocks, no coding required. The free plan is limited; paid plans start at ~$15/month.

**LPgenerator, Landingi** — alternatives with A/B testing capabilities.

**WordPress + Elementor** — more flexible but takes longer to set up.

**Rule of thumb:** For your first custom landing page — use Tilda. It’s simpler and faster.

teach.title: Adapting Someone Else's Landing Page
teach.body:
I found a competitor’s successful landing page using Spy → downloaded the HTML code → adapted it: changed the text, images, and form.

Basic knowledge of HTML is required [→ Lesson 10.7]. You don’t need to understand the entire code—just find the element you need and change it.

Important: Replace ALL content with your own unique content (text, images, product name). Do not use other people’s photos or reviews.

teach.title: AI for Landing Page Copy
teach.body:
Claude or ChatGPT can write copy for a landing page:

Prompt template: "Write a landing page text for [product], target audience [description], main problem [pain point], benefit [result], proof [type], CTA [action]. Structure: headline, subheadline, 5 benefits, 3 testimonials, CTA. Language: [Polish/Ukrainian]."

Once you receive the text, edit and adapt it. The AI provides a good foundation but needs to be refined to fit the specifics of your niche.

teach.title: Pre-launch Checklist for the Landing Page
teach.body:
- [ ] Mobile load time: up to 3 seconds
- [ ] Domain verified via the Facebook Sharing Debugger
- [ ] Test lead submitted and data received in the affiliate CRM
- [ ] The mobile version is correct—the button is visible without scrolling
- [ ] Message Match with creatives—the headline matches the ad’s promise
- [ ] The pixel is installed and the “Lead” event is triggered

l1.q: A newcomer has set up their first offer. Where can I get a landing page for my first test?
options: Create your own right away on Tilda
Use a ready-made landing page from the affiliate program
Download a competitor's landing page using Spy
Order from a layout artist

l1.q: A media buyer took a landing page from an affiliate network without checking the loading speed. The page takes 8 seconds to load. What will happen?
options: Facebook automatically optimizes loading speed
Most mobile users will close the page before it finishes loading—the conversion rate will be critically low
Speed doesn't matter if the créole is strong
This is only a problem with a slow internet connection

Scenario A: A newcomer, first offer, $100 budget, no time for development.
Situation B: Experienced buyer, profitable offer, 1.7% conversion rate on the affiliate landing page, wants to improve it.
Situation C: Found a successful competitor’s landing page via spy that’s been running for 3 months.

options: Traffic from an affiliate program
Analyzes the weaknesses in the affiliate's landing page and creates a better version of it on Tilda
Analyzes the structure, headings, and approaches—then creates a custom landing page using the same principles but with new text and images

options: Traffic from an affiliate program
Analyzes the weaknesses in the affiliate's landing page and creates a better version of it on Tilda

lessons.title: Speed and Technical Optimization of the Landing Page

teach.title: Why Speed Equals Money
teach.body:
Every second of loading time means conversions you didn’t get. According to Google, when load time increases from 1 to 3 seconds, the likelihood of bounce increases by 32%. From 1 to 5 seconds—by 90%.

This is especially critical for mobile traffic (80%+ in affiliate marketing). Mobile internet is slower, and the audience’s attention span is shorter.

**Speed Goals:**
- Up to 2 seconds — excellent
- 2–3 seconds — acceptable
- 3–5 seconds — noticeable CR losses (~20–40%)
- 5+ seconds — critical (~50–90% abandonment before loading)

teach.title: How to Check Your Speed
teach.body:
**Google PageSpeed Insights** (pagespeed.web.dev) — free. It provides a score (0–100) and specific recommendations on which elements are slowing down the page the most. Be sure to check the mobile version—it’s more critical.

**GTmetrix** (gtmetrix.com) — provides a more detailed analysis with a waterfall chart. It shows how long each element takes to load.

**Simple test:** Open the landing page on your phone using mobile data (not Wi-Fi) and time how long it takes.

teach.title: The Main Causes of a Slow Landing and How to Fix Them
teach.body:
**Large images (the most common cause)**
An unoptimized 5 MB image takes 3–5 seconds to load on a mobile device. When compressed to 200 KB, it loads in 0.3–0.5 seconds.

Compression tools:
- TinyPNG.com — free, for PNG and JPEG
- Squoosh.app (Google) — more flexible, supports WebP
- Rule: No image on the landing page should be larger than 200 KB. For background images—up to 100 KB.

**Server Far from the Audience**
If you’re targeting Poland but your hosting is in the U.S., every request travels across the ocean. The difference: 50 ms (Poland) vs. 200+ ms (U.S.). This is noticeable on mobile.

Solution: Hosting with servers in the EU (Poland, France, Germany). Providers: Hetzner (Finland/Germany), OVH (France/Poland), DigitalOcean (Amsterdam).

**Too Many Scripts**
Every additional plugin or script (analytics, chat, marketing tools) adds to the load time. Keep only what’s necessary: the Facebook pixel, basic analytics, and the affiliate pixel.

**Solutions that don’t require technical knowledge:**
If your landing page is on Tilda or a website builder, built-in optimization is available. Simply compress your images before uploading them and select the correct data center during setup.

teach.title: Mobile Optimization
teach.body:
Over 80% of traffic in affiliate marketing comes from mobile devices. If the landing page isn’t optimized for mobile, the conversion rate (CR) will be poor even with fast loading speeds.

What to check on mobile:
- The CTA button is visible without scrolling (above the fold)
- The order form displays correctly and is easy to fill out on a phone
- The text is readable without zooming
- Images aren’t cropped
- Buttons are large enough to tap with a finger (at least 44×44 px)

teach.title: Facebook Sharing Debugger
teach.body:
Tool: developers.facebook.com/tools/debug

Paste the landing page URL and you’ll see:
- Whether there are any issues with the domain (e.g., if it’s on a blacklist)
- What link preview will be shown in the ad (title, description, image)
- Whether there are errors with the meta tags

If the link preview isn’t displaying correctly, you can update the meta tags on the landing page and click “Scrape Again” in the Debugger.

l1.q: Google PageSpeed scored 25/100 for the mobile version. First step:
options: Keep — these ratings have no effect
Check which elements are causing the most slowdown and fix them (most often, these are large images)
Switch to another website builder
Order a new landing page

l1.q: You're targeting a Polish audience. Your site is hosted in the U.S. Is that a problem?
options: Polish users will not be able to access the website
The physical distance between the server and the user increases the loading time
Facebook does not allow U.S. hosting providers for Polish traffic
There are no problems

l2.situation:
Situation:
CTR 3.1% — good. CR 0.5% — bad. $200 in spending over the week, 4 conversions.

Checked:
- Google PageSpeed for mobile: 19/100, 9-second load time
- On a phone: the button isn’t visible without scrolling; the form extends beyond the screen
- Hosting: Singapore (target audience — Poland)

options: Slow loading only
Slow loading + poor mobile version + distant server—all three combined
Just a bad mobile version
Hosting does not affect CR

items: Compress the image (fastest and most effective)
Fix the mobile version (button above the fold, form is correct)
Transfer hosting to a Polish or EU server

lessons.title: Message Match: Matching the Creative and the Landing Page

teach.title: What is Message Match and why is it critical?
teach.body:
**Message Match** — the alignment between the ad’s message and what the user sees on the landing page.

A user clicks on an ad with certain expectations. If the landing page meets those expectations, they stay. If not, they leave within seconds. Most people decide whether to stay or leave within the first 3–5 seconds on the page.

A high bounce rate with a good CTR = a problem with Message Match.

teach.title: Common Issues and How to Fix Them
teach.body:
**Discrepancy 1: Different Types of Pain**
Creation: A woman with knee pain
Landing page headline: "Remedy for joint and back pain"

Correction: “Get rid of knee pain—results after just one week”

**Discrepancy 2: Discount Promise Not Fulfilled**
Creative: “40% off today only”
Landing page: full price or a different discount

Correction: either remove the discount from the creative or add a real discount to the landing page

**Discrepancy 3: Different Target Audience**
Creative: Women 55+ (“for people of mature age”)
Landing Page: A young person in the main photo

Correction: Replace the main image with one appropriate for the target audience

**Discrepancy 4: Different Tone**
Creative: Emotional, based on personal pain
Landing page: Cold, medical text with technical terminology

Correction: Adapt the landing page text to match the tone of the creative

**Discrepancy 5: Different Product or Offer**
The creative refers to one product (pills), but the landing page sells another (cream)

Correction: Always verify that the creative and landing page refer to the same product and offer

teach.title: How to Check Message Match
teach.body:
A simple test: Ask someone who isn’t familiar with the campaign to:
1. Watch the ad (10–15 seconds)
2. Immediately open the landing page
3. Ask: “Did you expect to see exactly this? What’s different here from the ad?”

If the person notices discrepancies—they’re definitely there.

Technical approach: Compare key elements systematically:

| Element | In the ad | On the landing page | Match |
|---------|--------|----------|---------------|
| Specific pain | knees | joints in general | ❌ |
| Discount | 30% | 30% | ✓ |
| Character | woman 55+ | woman 55+ | ✓ |
| Time to results | 10 days | 7–14 days | ~ |

l1.q: Creo: "Free shipping today." Land: 50 UAH shipping fee. What will happen?
options: People won't notice the difference between "creo" and "land"
The gap between promises and reality will erode trust, and most people will turn the page
People will order it anyway because it's a good product
Facebook will block ads

l1.q: Creo for women ages 45–60 who experience back pain after work. Landing page headline: “An effective pain reliever for everyone.” What’s the problem?
options: The title is too short
A general headline does not confirm a specific report by Creo
The word "effective" sounds too much like an advertising slogan
No problem

l2.situation:
Situation:
CTR: 2.7% (good). CR: 0.6% (poor). CPA: $30 with a payout of $8.

Creative: 25-second video, a 55-year-old woman who can’t bend over, text: “Do your knees hurt? Get rid of the pain in 7 days with a 40% discount”

Landing Page:
- Headline: “FlexiJoint — Joint Relief”
- Subheadline: “Natural ingredients, clinically tested”
- Image: anatomical diagram of a joint
- Form: first name, last name, email, phone number, city, ZIP code
- Button: “Submit Request”
- No discount

questions.q: All issues with Message Match and conversions:
options: The headline does not mention the knees and does not support KREO
The 40% discount is not available on the landing page
The anatomical diagram is impersonal; it doesn't convey any emotional tone.
Too many fields in the form
The "Submit Application" CTA is weak

questions.q: After the correction, the CR rose to 3.5%. What about the CPA now?
options: The CPA will remain unchanged
CPA will decrease by about 5 to 6 times (0.6% → 3.5%)—the same clicks now convert much better
CPA will increase
CPA depends solely on the payment

questions.q: The first step after fixing the landing page:
options: Increase the budget immediately
Run a test using the same creative and the revised landing page to see if the CR has actually improved
Change both the creative and the landing page at the same time
Ask the manager for a bump

summary:
After completing this module, the student will:

- Understand the difference between a landing page and a pre-landing page, and when each is needed
- Know the structure of a high-converting landing page: from the headline to the CTA
- Understand the types of pre-landing pages (articles, quizzes) and why they should look like editorial content
- Know where to source landing pages and how to properly prepare them for launch
- Be able to test page speed and fix the main causes of slow landing pages
- Understand Message Match and be able to identify gaps between creative and landing pages

**Next module:** Launch, optimization, and basic analytics.
